new.title: Tour Schloss Charlottenburg and its garden
new.desc: The baroque palace that gave Charlottenburg its name is the biggest surviving royal residence in Berlin, with a formal garden running down to the Spree behind it.
new.tip: The palace garden is free to wander, so come for a walk even if you skip the state rooms.

new.title: Step into the blue light of the Gedächtniskirche
new.desc: The bombed stump of the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church was left standing as a warning, and the 1960s octagonal chapel beside it glows deep blue inside from thousands of glass blocks.
new.tip: Visit both halves: the old tower hall has the memorial exhibition and surviving mosaics, the new chapel has the light.

new.title: Climb the 285 steps of the Siegessäule
new.desc: The Victory Column stands in the middle of the Großer Stern roundabout, topped by the gilded Victoria that Berliners call Goldelse. From the platform the Tiergarten spreads out in every direction.
new.tip: Do not cross the traffic: go down through one of the four little gatehouses and use the pedestrian tunnel. There is no lift.

new.title: Find the Vermeers in the Gemäldegalerie
new.desc: One of the world's great Old Master collections hangs at the Kulturforum, with Caravaggio's Amor Victorious, two Vermeers, a room of Rembrandts and five Raphael Madonnas.
new.tip: It is far quieter than Museum Island. Pick a few rooms instead of trying all of them in one go.

new.title: Admire the glass temple of the Neue Nationalgalerie
new.desc: Mies van der Rohe's steel and glass pavilion from 1968 is a work of art in itself, carefully restored by David Chipperfield and reopened in 2021 with 20th century art inside.
new.tip: Walk around the terrace and look for the sculpture garden at the back, with works by Calder, Moore and Serra.

new.title: Meet Helmut Newton at the Museum für Fotografie
new.desc: A former officers' casino behind Bahnhof Zoo houses the Helmut Newton Foundation and changing photography shows from the state museums.
new.tip: Combine it with C/O Berlin around the corner for a full afternoon of photography.

new.title: Go Art Nouveau at the Bröhan-Museum
new.desc: Opposite Schloss Charlottenburg, this small museum is packed with Jugendstil and Art Deco furniture, glass and porcelain arranged like lived-in rooms.
new.tip: The Scharf-Gerstenberg collection of Surrealist art is right across the street if you want a second museum.

new.title: Stand where Kennedy said 'Ich bin ein Berliner'
new.desc: Rathaus Schöneberg was West Berlin's city hall during the division, and it was from its steps that John F. Kennedy gave his famous speech in 1963.
new.tip: The square in front is now John-F.-Kennedy-Platz. The Ratskeller in the building serves old-school German food.

new.title: Read the lamppost signs in the Bayerisches Viertel
new.desc: Around Bayerischer Platz, small signs on the lampposts quote the Nazi laws that stripped Jewish neighbours of their rights one by one. It is one of Berlin's quietest and most unsettling memorials.
new.tip: Start at U Bayerischer Platz and simply walk the side streets, reading both sides of each sign.

new.title: See contemporary art at Hamburger Bahnhof
new.desc: A 19th century railway terminus on the edge of Moabit is now the national gallery for contemporary art, with huge installations in the old train hall.
new.tip: It is a short walk from Hauptbahnhof, handy if you have an hour or two before a train.

new.title: Pay your respects at Gedenkstätte Plötzensee
new.desc: In this plain brick shed the Nazi justice system executed thousands of people, among them many members of the resistance. The memorial is small, stark and hard to forget.
new.tip: It sits in an industrial corner of Charlottenburg-Nord. Take the bus to Gedenkstätte Plötzensee and allow half an hour.

new.title: Walk into the Olympiastadion
new.desc: Built for the 1936 Games, the monumental stadium is a heavy piece of Nazi-era architecture that today hosts Hertha BSC and the German cup final.
new.tip: Go up the Glockenturm next door for a view over the stadium, the Maifeld and the Grunewald.

new.title: Graze through the KaDeWe food hall
new.desc: The sixth floor of the Kaufhaus des Westens is a legend: counter after counter of oysters, sausages, cheese, pralines and cakes, with bar stools to eat on the spot.
new.tip: Sit down at one of the counters for a glass and a plate instead of only looking. Weekday mornings are calmest.

new.title: Snack your way round the Winterfeldtmarkt
new.desc: Schöneberg's market on Winterfeldtplatz is the most loved weekly market in Berlin, with farm produce, flowers and plenty of stalls selling things to eat right away.
new.tip: Market days are Wednesday and Saturday. Saturday is the big one, so come hungry before noon.

new.title: Have lunch in the Arminiusmarkthalle
new.desc: Moabit's handsome brick market hall from the 1890s now mixes traditional stalls with food counters, cafés and bars under its iron roof.
new.tip: Closed on Sundays. Come at lunchtime and pick a different stall for each course.

new.title: Drink a beer by the water at Café am Neuen See
new.desc: Hidden among the trees of the Tiergarten, this lakeside beer garden calls itself probably the prettiest traditional Biergarten in Berlin, and on a warm evening it is hard to argue.
new.tip: Rowing boats are usually for hire at the lake in summer. Find a table at the water's edge.
new.q: Café am Neuen See, Lichtensteinallee 2, Berlin

new.title: Eat Thai street food at the Thaipark market
new.desc: What began as Thai families picnicking on the lawn of the Preußenpark grew into Berlin's best known street food market: papaya salad, noodle soups, skewers and mango sticky rice cooked by home cooks.
new.tip: The market moved off the lawn in 2024 to Württembergische Straße next to the park, and may move again. It runs at weekends in the warm months, near U Fehrbelliner Platz.

new.title: Have breakfast in the Literaturhaus garden
new.desc: The café of the Literaturhaus sits in a 19th century villa on leafy Fasanenstraße, with a winter garden, a front garden and properly dressed waiters.
new.tip: Ask for a table in the garden on a sunny morning, then stroll down Fasanenstraße, one of the prettiest side streets off the Ku'damm.

new.title: Sip Riesling at the Rheingauer Weinbrunnen
new.desc: Every summer since 1967, winegrowers from the Rheingau have taken turns pouring their wines on Rüdesheimer Platz in Wilmersdorf, and the whole neighbourhood turns up.
new.tip: Bringing your own picnic is the done thing. Grab a spot near the Siegfried fountain.

new.title: Order breakfast at midnight in Schwarzes Café
new.desc: This rambling café near Savignyplatz has been open almost around the clock since 1978. It is a café by day, a bar at night and a West Berlin institution at any hour.
new.tip: Head upstairs for the nicest rooms. It only shuts for a few hours early on Tuesday mornings.

new.title: Eat like old West Berlin at Diener Tattersall
new.desc: A wood-panelled artists' pub off Savignyplatz serving plain German cooking, the kind of place where actors and painters have long ended their evenings.
new.tip: Come late, after the theatre, when the room is at its liveliest.

new.title: Enter Zoo Berlin through the Elephant Gate
new.desc: Germany's oldest zoo opened in 1844 and keeps more species than almost any other in the world, including the country's only giant pandas.
new.tip: Use the Elephant Gate on Budapester Straße, next to the Aquarium, rather than the entrance by the station.

new.title: Catch a free lunch concert at the Philharmonie
new.desc: On Wednesdays at lunchtime, musicians play chamber music in the foyer of Hans Scharoun's golden concert hall, and anyone can walk in and listen.
new.tip: Arrive at least 45 minutes early: once the foyer is full, nobody else gets in. The series pauses in July and August.

new.title: Hunt for treasure at the Straße des 17. Juni flea market
new.desc: Every weekend the boulevard between S Tiergarten and the Charlottenburger Tor fills with antiques, old Berlin postcards, silverware and vinyl, with an arts and crafts market on the far side of the gate.
new.tip: This is the pricier, more serious kind of flea market, so haggle politely and come early for the best pieces.

new.title: See a photo show at C/O Berlin
new.desc: The 1950s Amerika Haus by Bahnhof Zoo is home to C/O Berlin, which stages some of the best photography exhibitions in the country.
new.tip: Shows change every few months, so check what is on. Galerie Camera Work on Kantstraße is another stop for photo fans.
new.q: C/O Berlin, Amerika Haus, Hardenbergstraße 22, Berlin

new.title: Spend an evening in the Bar jeder Vernunft mirror tent
new.desc: A wooden Spiegelzelt built in 1912 stands on a parking deck in Wilmersdorf and has hosted chanson, cabaret and musical comedy since 1992, with guests seated at little tables and in velvet booths.
new.tip: Most shows are in German, but concerts and music nights work in any language. There is a beer garden outside in summer.

new.title: Watch a film in the Zoo Palast
new.desc: For decades this 1957 cinema was the main stage of the Berlinale. Restored with its sweeping curtain and plush seats, it is still the most glamorous place in the city to see a film.
new.tip: Afterwards walk through Bikini Berlin next door: its roof terrace looks straight into the zoo's monkey enclosure.

new.title: Walk the overgrown rails of Natur-Park Südgelände
new.desc: A railway yard in Schöneberg was abandoned after the war and nature took over. Today raised walkways lead past birch woods, rusting tracks, an old steam engine and a water tower.
new.tip: The entrance is right at S Priesterweg. Stay on the walkways, as the wild parts are protected.

new.title: Browse the bookshop under the tracks at Savignyplatz
new.desc: Savignyplatz is the living room of old West Berlin, a leafy square ringed by cafés and restaurants. In the railway arches beside it, an art bookshop trades while the S-Bahn rumbles overhead.
new.tip: Follow the arches along the passage towards Bleibtreustraße for more small shops and bars.

new.title: Do a lap of the Lietzensee
new.desc: A narrow lake in a sunken park, lined with grand Charlottenburg apartment houses, where locals jog, picnic and feed the ducks far from any tour group.
new.tip: After your walk, browse the antique shops on nearby Suarezstraße, known as the Antikmeile.

new.title: Climb the Juliusturm at Zitadelle Spandau
new.desc: Spandau's moated Renaissance fortress is one of the best preserved in Europe. Inside you will find the medieval Juliusturm, a bat cellar and a hall of toppled Berlin monuments, including the giant granite head of Lenin.
new.tip: The tower has 153 steps and a view over Spandau and the Havel. Take the U7 to Zitadelle.

new.title: See Mielke's office at the Stasimuseum
new.desc: House 1 of the former Stasi headquarters in Lichtenberg is frozen in time: the wood-panelled office suite of minister Erich Mielke is exactly as he left it, alongside spy cameras and surveillance files.
new.tip: Take the U5 to Magdalenenstraße. Public tours in English run on most afternoons.

new.title: Wander the brick ruins of Kloster Chorin
new.desc: This Cistercian abbey, founded in 1258 in the woods of the Barnim, is a textbook piece of North German Brick Gothic. Schinkel saved the roofless church from collapse in the 19th century.
new.tip: Take the regional train from Berlin to Chorin station and walk through the forest to the abbey. Summer weekends often bring open-air concerts.

new.title: Visit the Sachsenhausen memorial in Oranienburg
new.desc: Sachsenhausen was the model concentration camp, laid out as a triangle so that one tower could oversee everything. The memorial tells the story of the Nazi camp and of the Soviet special camp that followed.
new.tip: Take the S1 or a regional train to Oranienburg, then walk about 20 minutes or take the bus. Allow at least three hours.
new.q: Gedenkstätte Sachsenhausen, Straße der Nationen 22, Oranienburg

new.title: See Schloss Rheinsberg mirrored in its lake
new.desc: The young Frederick the Great called his years in this lakeside rococo palace the happiest of his life, and it became the blueprint for Sanssouci. It also houses a museum to Kurt Tucholsky, who set a love story here.
new.tip: Walk round the Grienericksee to the obelisk for the classic view back to the palace. Rheinsberg is about 100 km north of Berlin, easiest by car.

new.title: Find the Antichrist window in Frankfurt (Oder)
new.desc: The huge brick Marienkirche in Frankfurt (Oder) holds a rarity: medieval stained glass telling the life of the Antichrist, picture by picture, like a 14th century comic strip.
new.tip: Regional trains from Berlin take a little over an hour. Afterwards walk across the Oder bridge to Słubice in Poland for coffee.

new.title: Slurp pho at the Dong Xuan Center
new.desc: Named after Hanoi's great market, this cluster of wholesale halls in Lichtenberg is Berlin's Little Vietnam, with fabric, plastic flowers, nail salons and canteens serving noodle soup to the traders.
new.tip: Take tram M8 or 21 to Herzbergstraße/Industriegebiet. The halls are usually closed on Tuesdays.

new.title: Drink unfiltered beer in the Eschenbräu courtyard
new.desc: Tucked into a housing block in Wedding, this small brewery pours its own Pils, Dunkel and Hefeweizen, plus a changing seasonal brew, under old trees. The beer is sold nowhere else.
new.tip: Order a Flammkuchen with your beer, or bring your own picnic, which is welcome in the garden.

new.title: Taste Schwarzer Abt at the Neuzelle monastery brewery
new.desc: Beer has been brewed beside the baroque abbey of Neuzelle since 1589. The dark, sweetish Schwarzer Abt triggered a 13 year legal fight over whether it could be called beer at all, which the brewery won.
new.tip: Visit the lavish abbey church next door too. By train, change at Frankfurt (Oder) for Neuzelle.

new.title: Have cake in the courtyard of Mutter Fourage
new.desc: An old fodder merchant's yard in Wannsee village has become a charming mix of courtyard café, plant nursery, gallery and delicatessen, more than a century after it was built.
new.tip: Take the S-Bahn to Wannsee and a bus to Rathaus Wannsee. It pairs well with a walk along the lake.

new.title: Explore the spy station on the Teufelsberg
new.desc: The Teufelsberg is a hill made of war rubble piled over an unfinished Nazi college. On top stand the torn radar domes of a Cold War listening station, now covered floor to ceiling in street art.
new.tip: Walk up through the Grunewald from S Heerstraße. The neighbouring Drachenberg is free and has a great sunset view.

new.title: Ride the cable car over the Gärten der Welt
new.desc: Among the tower blocks of Marzahn lies a park of gardens from around the globe, with Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Balinese and Oriental gardens, and a cable car gliding over the Kienberg hill.
new.tip: Take the U5 to Kienberg and float in by cable car. The cable car ticket is separate from normal public transport tickets.
new.q: Gärten der Welt, Blumberger Damm 44, Berlin

new.title: Walk under the Spree to the Müggelsee
new.desc: Berlin's biggest lake lies out east in Köpenick. In Friedrichshagen, a pedestrian tunnel dips beneath the river right where it leaves the lake and brings you out onto the wooded southern shore.
new.tip: Take the S3 to Friedrichshagen and stroll down Bölschestraße to the water. Excursion boats cross the lake in summer.

new.title: Watch ships ride the lift at Niederfinow
new.desc: At Niederfinow in the Barnim, a steel giant from 1934 raises and lowers whole ships 36 metres in about five minutes. A new, even bigger lift opened beside it in 2022, so you can now watch two.
new.tip: Take the train to Eberswalde and continue by bus or bike along the canal. Excursion boats usually take passengers through the lift in season.

new.title: Soak in the thermal brine at Bad Saarow
new.desc: Bad Saarow on the Scharmützelsee has been a spa town for a century, and Maxim Gorky once came here to recover. The SaarowTherme fills its pools with warm salty water from deep underground.
new.tip: Take the regional express to Fürstenwalde and change for the short branch line to Bad Saarow. Walk the lakeside promenade before your soak.
